articles.title: Ebola spreads to 60 health zones in eastern DRC; UN warns of funding shortfall
articles.author: Pavan Kulkarni
articles.content: The fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history, killing nearly one in two infected in the eastern region of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), has spread to six new health zones between August 14 and August 28. The spread remains within six of the country’s 26 provinces identified before August 14: namely Bas-Uélé, Haut-Uélé, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, and Tshopo. However, the number of health zones affected within these six provinces increased from 54 of the 151 to 60 over the following two weeks. The spread was identified in a new health zone of the Tshopo province on August 15. By August 23, the spread was also confirmed in Viadana in Bas-Uélé and Mutwanga in North Kivu. On August 28, infections were also confirmed in the Ganga health zone of Bas-Uélé as well as in Biena and Manguredjipa in North Kivu. The Rwandan army and its front, the M23 armed group, which are waging a war for DRC’s mineral wealth, have occupied large areas of North Kivu province, where the case fatality rate (CFR) is 68.6% , significantly higher than the overall CFR of 48.1%. In just over three months since the outbreak was officially declared on May 15, the disease had infected 5,794 people in DRC as of August 26, killing 2,786 of them. This outbreak is the “fastest-spreading Ebola epidemic ever recorded,” the UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said on August 27. “It’s growing faster and wider than the response to contain it.” The effectiveness of the response is complicated by a combination of factors – importantly, armed conflict involving multiple groups, large concentrations of displaced populations, a mobile labor force working in mines, poor infrastructure, and a lack of public trust sparking attacks on medical facilities. And then there is a severe shortage of funds. Guterres told reporters at the UN HQ that the humanitarian response is only 48% funded. “Without additional funding, vital operations will run out of money at the very moment they need to ramp up,” he warned . Resources currently available for the response “will last only weeks, not months,” the UN warned. “We know how to contain Ebola, how to interrupt transmission and how to save lives, but we must also overcome another virus: the virus of indifference,” said Guterres.

articles.title: Mutiny crushed in Niger; normalcy returns as AES reaffirms unity
articles.author: Pavan Kulkarni
articles.content: Civil society groups marched in solidarity with Niger’s military government on Sunday, August 30, after the army suppressed a mutiny overnight at the country’s main air base in the capital, Niamey, restoring normalcy by Saturday morning. Thousands of people march in solidarity with the CNSP as it faced a mutiny. Photo: ANP Gunfire and explosions were also heard at some sensitive military sites in Niamey after the mutiny began around 20 minutes past midnight , with a group of soldiers confining other soldiers to their barracks and holding them hostage in the military base 101. The base is located in the compound of the Diori Hamani International Airport, about a kilometer away from civilian infrastructure. However, the airport itself was not affected, and flights continued normally, the director general of the National Civil Aviation Agency (ANAC) said . TV and radio broadcasts were interrupted, but resumed by 10 am. “The prompt reaction of the defense and security forces made it possible to contain this unrest and gradually regain control of these sites,” Defense Minister Salifou Modi said in a statement broadcast on state television. “Vehicular traffic was normal by morning. People went to work. Shops, businesses, and schools were open. Even civil service exams scheduled for the day went ahead as planned,” said Aboubakar Alassane, a leader of the West Africa Peoples Organization (WAPO). Several mutinous soldiers were arrested later in the day. Authorities are reportedly on the hunt for Lieutenant Moutari Yahaya, who is on the run after alleged involvement in the mutiny. “Some who had escaped from base 101 after the failure of the mutiny were hiding in the neighboring residential areas. However, residents mobilized to catch them and hand them over to the military authorities,” said Abdullahi Salifou, deputy secretary of the Convergence for the Sovereignty of Sahelian Nations (COSNAS). Emerging from mass protests against the continued domination of Niger by its former colonizer France, COSNAS was formed after the regime of Mohamed Bazoum, widely perceived in the country as a puppet of France, was overthrown in a popular military coup in 2023. Read more: Thousands rally in support of Niger’s coup leaders as Western-backed ECOWAS threatens military intervention The subsequent military government, led by General Abdourahamane Tiani, which expelled the French troops from the country, has since repeatedly accused France of attempting to destabilize the country using terror groups. Other members of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES), Mali and Burkina Faso, which had also expelled French troops under similar circumstances, have also made the same accusation. Read more: France is a state sponsor of terror, AES countries declare However, Alassane said, it is unlikely that France engineered this mutiny. “I don’t think it was a coup attempt, because there was no attack on the Presidential Palace, which would have been the target if the rebelling soldiers had tried to take power. There was no heavy barricading outside the Presidential Palace when I passed nearby the next day. Base 101 is seven kilometers away.” He opined that this mutiny, which was limited to this base and a few other sites, was provoked by discontent among a section of soldiers caused by the harsh conditions of life and work imposed by the constant struggle against terror groups allegedly backed by France. Read more: 13 killed in terror attack on airport, Niger’s defense ministry alleges participation of France-backed mercenaries “Supporters of Bazoum’s regime residing in France are spreading on social media” an interpretation of this mutiny as a generational rift within the army, with the younger officers rebelling against their seniors. “But that is not true,” said Alassane, arguing that the military in Niger is a generational profession. “Most young officers are sons and grandsons of generals, colonels – many of them still serving.” Calling “on the people of Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger to remain vigilant against disinformation campaigns, manipulation of opinion and attempts at division”, the AES reaffirmed its determination to preserve “the unity, cohesion and stability of the confederal space.” Its statement praised the “bravery and professionalism” with which “the loyalist republican forces” of Niger had acted to contain the mutiny quickly. Niger’s northern neighbor, Algeria, with which it had reset diplomatic relations earlier this year after previous tensions, also condemned the mutiny as “highly regrettable.” It said in a statement that “as soon as it became aware of these events, Algeria assured the highest authorities of Niger of its full solidarity and firm support, with a view to overcoming this ordeal and promoting a rapid return to stability in this brotherly country.” Later, Algeria deployed four Sukhoi Su-30 fighter jets to Niger to support the Nigerian Armed Forces against “the attempt to destabilize the fraternal country of Niger.” Read more: Algeria provides Niger with helicopters and military equipment as bilateral ties improve

articles.title: Will a new political alliance unseat the Abbas-led Palestinian Authority?
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: After over two decades of political impasse caused by the division between the major Palestinian factions Fatah and Hamas, a new alliance in the making has revealed itself as a national unity coalition. The coalition will participate in the historic November 28 elections for the Palestinian Legislative Council (PLC). The PLC elections were held in 2006. According to media reports, the emerging election coalition comprises the Fatah-affiliated Democratic Reform Current and led by Mohammad Dahlan, Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad, the Popular Resistance Committees, and Nasser al-Qudwa’s National Democratic Forum. The Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) and the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine (DFLP) have yet to finalize their decision to join the coalition, reports indicate. A controversial alliance that would end the Abbas era The news regarding the nascent alliance drew mixed reaction among the Palestinian grassroots, and provoked the indignation of the Fatah bloc led by the President of the Palestinian Authority (PA) Mahmoud Abbas. For over two decades, the Abbas-led Palestinian Authority has sought to tighten its grip on the political landscape in the occupied West Bank. Since Hamas’s landslide victory in 2006, the PA has manuevered to maintain control by repeatedly blocking presidential and legislative elections and obstructing reconciliation efforts with Hamas. The PA has also brutally cracked down on its opponents in the West Bank through detention, administrative restrictions, and in some cases assassinations , with greater focus placed on members of Hamas. However, this crackdown has even extended to include members of the Fatah movement. In 2011, Abbas suspended Mohammad Dahlan from Fatah over alleged corruption and coup plotting. Dahlan then moved into exile in the United Arab Emirates, but his supporters in the West Bank were frequently targeted by the PA security forces. For many, Abbas has sidelined Dahlan and his entourage because he posed a significant political threat as a prospective successor, a fear which now seems to have manifested. Furthermore, the Abbas administration has systematically suppressed cross-factional resistance groups in the West Bank in collaboration with the Israeli forces, in order to sustain the US-backed security coordination process with Israel. Read more: In collaboration with the US, Israel, Palestinian Authority escalates crackdown on resistance in West Bank The Abbas era has been marked by economic recession, growing corruption, and deterioration in security. Moreover, his administration is blamed for further worsening Gaza’s humanitarian crisis – already exacerbated by the Israeli siege – by implementing punitive financial measures against the Hamas-run government in the besieged Strip between 2017 and 2018. Analysts argue that all these factors, along with its submissive stance toward the Israeli genocidal aggression on Gaza, have led to a sharp decline in the PA’s popularity among Palestinians. Political activist and former prisoner in Israeli jails, Omar Assaf, argues that the new coalition has drawn controversy due to the historic disparity between the factions it comprises, particularly their position on crucial issues such as armed resistance against the occupation and the Oslo Accords. From Assaf’s point of view, this alliance was formed out of necessity or compulsion as the only solution to counter the monopoly of Abbas’s bloc. He added that the Palestinian Popular Conference (14 Million), where he serves as a coordinator, joined another alliance in the West Bank to run in the upcoming elections. “These alliances will diminish the Palestinian Authority’s chances of securing an overwhelming victory in the elections. Recent polls show that the PA’s popularity among Palestinians has declined to 10–15%, meaning the bloc representing the PA is expected to win only around 15 out of 132 seats in the upcoming elections.” Assaf noted. Read more: Israel has used the Oslo Accords to strengthen its occupation Mohammad Dahlan: the US-backed political leader for the next era Mohammad Dahlan , who seemingly leads the new coalition, constitutes another major aspect of this controversy. For many, he had played a key role in fueling the division, which led to a bloody infighting between Hamas and Fatah in Gaza in 2007. Many also say that the exiled Fatah leader became a key advisor to the rulers of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Saudi Arabia. He is therefore accused of allegedly having participated in instigating turmoil, internal conflict, and regime change across West Asia and Africa. Furthermore, analysts suggest that Dahlan receives substantial backing from the United States , with reports indicating his close contact with the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), and the Israel Security Agency (also known as Shin Bet). In addition, he is viewed by many as one of the former PA officials who established the rules of security coordination with the Israeli authorities, which a large segment of the Palestinian people opposes. Some sources claim that Dahlan succeeded in convincing Hamas to accept the disarmament plan proposed by Trump’s Board of Peace (BoP). This acceptance was meant to guarantee Hamas a role in the political Palestinian landscape. The claim was supported by an announcement made by the High Representative of the BoP, Nikolay Mladenov, on Wednesday, August 26, stating that Hamas and other resistance factions agreed “for the first time to surrender their weapons” and transfer full civilian and security authority to a UN-recognized transitional administration. If proven to be the case, the move may undermine the popularity of these factions among the Palestinian grassroots, after they had firmly insisted that they would not lay down arms under US pressure throughout the three-year Gaza ceasefire negotiations. Read more: Palestinian factions: We categorically reject unilateral disarmament The alliance has alarmed the PA While Dahlan continues to be a controversial figure, the new alliance still managed to alarm the Ramallah-based ruling class, seemingly pushing it towards taking counter-maneuvers in a desperate attempt to maintain its power, a power its leaders had long assumed to be infinite. A high-ranking Fatah delegation headed by the Palestinian Authority’s Vice President Hussein al-Sheikh traveled to Cairo last week to meet with Egyptian officials and representatives of the Dahlan-led bloc. Although the delegation was set to meet Hamas leaders in the Egyptian capital, the meeting was reportedly cancelled. The meetings ostensibly aim to unite the Fatah movement and enhance efforts for achieving reconciliation with other Palestinian factions. However, Al-Sheikh’s maneuvers were interpreted by commentators as a political survival effort by the PA. Dahlan jeopardizes the authority of the Abbas oligarchy as he seems to enjoy more substantial support from the United States, while maintaining a loyal network of supporters by pumping millions of dollars from the UAE into Gaza, the West Bank, and Palestinian refugee camps. With just three months left until the polls, the situation on the ground is bound to intensify as the different factions struggle to make political overtures and maneuver for votes amid intensified Israeli siege.

articles.title: When the mountain broke: inside Nepal’s deadliest Himalayan flood
articles.author: Madhab Pant
articles.content: At roughly 8:30 am on August 26, 2026, a wall of water, mud, ice, and massive boulders roared down the Lhende Khola into the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems. The surge struck without local rainfall or warning sirens, catching border communities like Timure, mid-morning. Initial reports mistook the ground tremors for an earthquake, but satellite and seismic data later confirmed the real trigger: a high-altitude collapse of rock and ice near Langtang Lirung, on the Tibetan side, spanning nearly one square kilometer and generating a ground shock equivalent to a magnitude 5.2 quake. Plunging 1,200 vertical meters into the valley, the avalanche briefly dammed the Lhende River before rupturing, unleashing a debris-laden slurry that tore through Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha, Tanahun, and Chitwan. Environmental drivers and hydrological cascade The disaster exposed the extreme fragility of high-altitude Himalayan ecosystems under a shifting climate. Rising temperatures and accelerating freeze-thaw cycles are steadily degrading permafrost and the cryogenic bonds that hold mountain bedrock together, priming slopes for collapse. This was not an isolated event: smaller glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) incidents in July 2025 had already weakened local topsoil and riverbank integrity. The catastrophe unfolded in two stages. First, the avalanche formed a short-lived debris dam across the narrow Lhende Khola. Hydrostatic pressure built rapidly behind the ice-and-rock wall as glacial meltwater and river discharge backed up, until the barrier gave way. Second, the released surge raced downstream at speeds exceeding 75 km/h, scouring up topsoil, riverbed gravel, and boulders as it went and turning into a hyper-abrasive slurry that gouged riverbeds, stripped valley walls, and undercut mountain foundations across the Bhotekoshi, Trishuli, and Narayani corridors. Secondary barrier lakes are still forming along blocked upper tributaries, prompting fresh flood warnings downstream. Human toll and structural damage According to Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) and the Nepal Police, the toll on life and infrastructure has been devastating. Confirmed deaths have surpassed 669, with victims swept as far as Chitwan (248), Nawalparasi East (158), and Paschim Nawalparasi (75); some remains were recovered up to 240 kilometres away in India’s Uttar Pradesh. Between 1,000 and 2,426 people remain missing, including 933 hydropower workers, dozens of security personnel from the Nepal Army, Police, and Armed Police Force, customs officers, residents, and over 500 foreign nationals mostly trekkers and Kailash Mansarovar pilgrims from more than 30 countries. On the recovery front, between 3,700 and 4,400 survivors have been treated or evacuated, including nearly 200 workers pulled from flooded underground hydropower tunnels. Damages are now estimated to exceed NRs 200 billion. The flood destroyed more than 80 bridges (35+ motorable, 45+ suspension) and washed out 40 kilometers of the vital Betrawati–Rasuwagadhi trade corridor, halting overland commerce with China. Thirteen run-of-the-river hydropower plants including the 111 MW Rasuwagadhi and 60 MW Upper Trishuli 3A sustained direct structural damage, knocking hundreds of megawatts off the national grid. Ecological disruption and human-made risk Beyond the human and economic cost, the scouring wiped out aquatic habitats and macroinvertebrate populations across Langtang National Park and its buffer zones. Millions of tons of topsoil were stripped from mountain slopes, while heavy silt deposits degraded farmland further downstream. Environmental assessments warn that unstable debris left in the upper tributaries could form new barrier lakes, raising the risk of further outburst floods when the rains return. Human activity in these narrow corridors amplified the destruction. Encroaching highway construction, constricted floodplains, and loose excavation muck from active building sites added extra material to the flood’s path. Once the surge hit, this debris and the narrowed riverbeds turned built infrastructure into secondary hazards that intensified the wave’s force. Emergency response and cross-border cooperation Nepal deployed over 15,000 security personnel from the Army, Police, and Armed Police Force alongside military and private helicopters for air-bridge evacuations, medical drops, and search operations. NDRRMA set up 12 Sector Coordination Teams to manage missing-person tracing, grid restoration, and aid delivery, backed by relief funds and truckloads of food, shelter, and medical supplies. Because high-altitude hazards cross borders, the response demanded fast regional coordination. China activated emergency protocols around Gyirong Port, sending over 500 rescue workers, while Chinese hydrological teams shared real-time water-level and barrier-lake satellite data with Nepal’s Flood Forecasting Division. In India, recovery operations ran in the border districts of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, gates at the Valmikinagar Barrage on the Gandak River were opened to manage surge volumes, and helplines were set up to trace missing pilgrims. The US, the IFRC, and global relief networks contributed emergency funding, shelter materials, traveler-tracking support, and diplomatic assistance for affected foreign nationals. Preventing a repeat of this scale of disaster will require stronger transboundary data-sharing, strictly enforced riparian buffer zones, comprehensive cumulative Environmental Impact Assessments for river-basin projects, and satellite-integrated early-warning networks built specifically for dynamic, high-altitude Himalayan conditions.

articles.title: “Catastrophe of Unimaginable Proportions”: Nepal Flood Death Toll Tops 900; Near 5,000 Still Missing
articles.content: More than 900 people in Nepal are confirmed dead after a massive wall of water, mud and debris crashed through a Himalayan river valley on the border with Tibet. More than 4,200 people are missing in Nepal and hundreds more in Tibet. Families are searching hospitals for loved ones, and crews have buried hundreds of unidentified bodies in shallow graves. Rescue efforts are also underway for more than 900 hydropower workers, believed to be trapped in more than a dozen underground tunnels blocked by debris. The cause of the flash flooding is believed to have been the collapse of a glacier in the mountains, leading a wave of water, rocks and debris to carve its way through the valley. “This is a catastrophe of unimaginable proportions,” says journalist Kunda Dixit, speaking to Democracy Now! from the Nepalese capital of Kathmandu. “We used to say that the glaciers are melting in the Himalaya. Now it seems like the mountains are cracking up,” says Dixit. “This has sort of redefined what global warming and climate change is doing, not just to Nepal and the Himalaya, but to the planet.”

articles.title: The Real Reason There’s a Munitions Shortage? Too Many Wars & a Dysfunctional Pentagon: William Hartung
articles.content: Top U.S. military leaders have reportedly advised Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth against extending the war in Iran because ongoing operations in the Middle East have degraded the Pentagon’s ability to confront threats elsewhere. According to The Washington Post , the warnings appeared in a classified assessment for Hegseth prepared by the heads of the Army, Navy and Air Force, and the four-star commanders overseeing U.S. operations throughout Europe, Asia and Latin America. This comes after multiple reports have revealed the U.S. is facing a critical munitions shortage, having used up much of its global stockpile of expensive missile systems during the war against Iran. “The Pentagon is completely dysfunctional when it comes to fighting this kind of war,” says defense analyst William Hartung, principal adviser at the Project on Government Oversight. He says the U.S. policy establishment and the defense industry are less interested in effectiveness than in running a “money-making machine.” Page 2 Thousands of residents recently spent two weeks without power in Gary, Indiana, following a storm that ripped through the majority-Black city. The blackout ground the city to a halt, trapping residents in their apartments, forcing the closure of many businesses and leading to fuel shortages at gas stations. Officials in Indiana estimate the storm might have caused up to $5 billion in damage in Gary and other communities. “We’re still in the recovery phase, as we speak,” says Gary Mayor Eddie Melton, who underscores that “hardening the infrastructure” should be a priority for the NIPSCO utility company. “We’ve never seen wind this strong before. … They need to ensure that the utility grid system is going to sustain that type of wind.” Page 3 As Gary, Indiana, recovers from flooding and a two-week power outage, we also speak with Ron Daniels, president of the Institute of the Black World 21st Century, who discusses the city’s history as a site of Black struggle and organizing. In 1972, the city hosted the National Black Political Convention, which brought together thousands of activists to plan for increasing African American political power. Attendees included Coretta Scott King, Betty Shabazz, Jesse Jackson, Bobby Seale, Louis Farrakhan, Shirley Chisholm, Harry Belafonte and Amiri Baraka. “It was one of the great gatherings in the history of Black people in this country,” says Daniels, who calls the current backlash to racial progress “the dying gasp of a system that needs a major overhaul.” Page 4 Tributes continue to pour in for Dolly Parton after the iconic country singer, actor and philanthropist’s death on August 25 at age 80. Her former co-star Jane Fonda tells Democracy Now! how they made the classic workplace comedy 9 to 5 , for which Parton wrote the accompanying hit song. “She could see through people to their essence,” Fonda says of Parton. “She loved everyone.” Topics Guests Please check back later for full transcript.

articles.title: “Don’t Be Squeamish About Squamous, Get a Checkup!” Amy Goodman’s Personal Health Update
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report . I’m Amy Goodman, with Juan González. Before we move on with the show, I wanted to say a few words about my absence from the show this week. I took time off following a minor but important medical procedure known as Mohs surgery — that’s M-O-H-S — microscopic surgery, to remove some skin cells on my nose that tested positive for squamous cell cancer. The procedure was painless, using only minimal local anesthesia, and it went well. I got the stitches out yesterday and now have Steri-Strips across the bridge of my nose, a kind of post-surgical Band-Aid. But I decided to come back on, because I think it’s important that we are not — you know, we don’t have to be picture-perfect on TV or video. We are not plastic; we are people. And people get by in all sorts of ways around the world, and I think it’s important not to hide. The good news is, in my case, we caught the problem in time. The medical team that treated me are confident they removed all the cancerous cells. And in medical terms, it means the edges are clear. And I’m really grateful to everyone here at Democracy Now! for covering me this week, especially my New York-based co-hosts Nermeen Shaikh and Anjali Kamat, our editorial director Mike Burke, who managed everything, Charina Nadura, Tey-Marie Astudillo — thank you so much — Deena Guzder, the whole team. And, Juan, of course, always thank you. It was a real treat watching the show from home with my dog Zazu by my side. I want to emphasize that the problem was caught in time, but too often people don’t realize that a spot, a bump on their skin, a mole or a blemish anywhere, or just a rough spot, something scaly, might be cancerous. We don’t have to be squeamish about squamous cell carcinoma or basal cell carcinoma, unless it’s not caught in time. Do your dermatology checks every year. And now with climate change, with the Earth heating, with the increased exposure to the sun, there’s an increase in skin cancer. And, Juan, as you so prophetically warned after the 9/11 attacks here in New York, the level of toxins downtown were devastating. And skin cancers, like squamous cell cancer, went way up, especially downtown. Back then, Democracy Now! was the closest national broadcast to ground zero, broadcasting from the firehouse studios of DCTV . Well, enough of this story. So, thanks again to everyone. It’s great to be back covering the important stories of the day.
